title: India's Inflation Just Breached the Central Bank's Red Line. The Iran War and a Weak Monsoon Are Making It Worse.
excerpt: Consumer prices are expected to have topped the RBI's 4 per cent target in June for the first time in sixteen months, with food, fuel and El Niño piling on pressure.
body:
India's consumer inflation likely breached the Reserve Bank of India's 4 per cent medium-term target in June for the first time in sixteen months, according to a Reuters poll of 37 economists, as higher food and fuel prices — amplified by the Iran war and a weak monsoon — squeezed household budgets from Delhi to Hyderabad.

The consumer price index is expected to have risen 4.3 per cent year-on-year in June, up from 3.93 per cent in May, with estimates ranging from 3.65 to 5.50 per cent. The official data is due on July 13. If confirmed, it would mark the highest inflation reading since India introduced its revised CPI series with a new base year and updated consumption basket in January.

## Food and Fuel: The Twin Squeeze

The inflation spike is not a surprise. State-owned fuel retailers raised petrol and diesel prices four times in May, feeding through to transportation and logistics costs across the economy. Brent crude has since surged further — gaining 5.5 per cent this week alone after renewed fighting between the United States and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz — pushing India's energy import bill higher still.

India imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil, making it the world's third-largest oil consumer. Every dollar added to the price of a barrel widens the current account deficit and raises costs for everything from cooking gas to auto-rickshaw fares.

Food prices, which carry the heaviest weight in India's CPI basket, have been climbing on the back of vegetable shortages and supply disruptions. Tomato and onion prices have spiked in several states, a politically sensitive development ahead of key state elections later this year.

## The El Niño Shadow

The monsoon, which irrigates over half of India's farmland, has been weaker than expected in parts of the northwest and central regions. Meteorologists are watching for signs of El Niño, the weather pattern associated with drier conditions across South and Southeast Asia.

If the monsoon underperforms, crop production of rice, pulses and oilseeds could fall, driving food inflation higher through the second half of the year. That would put the RBI in a bind: cut rates to support growth, or hold firm to anchor expectations.

## The RBI's Tightrope

The central bank held its key repo rate steady at 5.25 per cent at its June meeting, declining to tighten policy even as inflation concerns mounted. Governor Sanjay Malhotra has emphasised that the RBI's inflation-targeting framework aims for durable alignment with the 4 per cent target, not short-term reactions to volatile food and energy prices.

But the calculus is shifting. Before the June meeting, a majority of economists in a Reuters survey expected at least one rate hike by year-end. The foreign exchange market has added its own pressure: the rupee hit a record low of 96.96 per dollar in May before recovering to around 95.40, helped by RBI intervention and a package of measures to attract dollar inflows.

Those measures — including a swap window for foreign deposits and relaxed hedging rules — triggered a record $120 billion in corporate foreign exchange hedging in June, a sign that businesses are bracing for continued volatility.

## What Investors Abroad Should Watch

For NRI investors with exposure to Indian equities, bonds and real estate, the inflation trajectory matters on several fronts.

Higher inflation erodes real returns on fixed-income investments, including the government bonds that have attracted significant foreign flows. It also complicates the RBI's ability to cut rates in the future, which means the mortgage market — already stretched by pandemic-era property booms in Bangalore, Pune and Hyderabad — stays tight.

On the equity side, sectors sensitive to input costs — fast-moving consumer goods, automobiles and cement — typically underperform during inflationary episodes. IT services, which earn in dollars and face less domestic cost pressure, have historically been a relative haven.

The rupee's trajectory is equally important. A weaker rupee reduces the dollar value of NRI remittances and investments, though it benefits those sending money home from the United States or the Gulf. The RBI's intervention has created a temporary floor, but analysts warn that sustained high oil prices could erode that support.

The July 13 data release will set the tone. If inflation comes in at the higher end of estimates — above 4.5 per cent — expectations of a rate hike will crystallise, potentially weighing on markets in the short term but offering higher yields for patient investors.
